anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a log-pipeline bottleneck (generation, flush, switch, archive, or replication-retention of the redo stream) and a device-level I/O-throughput bottleneck on the same set of volumes, so both the engine’s ability to produce/consume log records and the physical storage’s ability to service any reads or writes are saturated at once.

Combined Phenomena: Commit latency, log-flush waits, and log-sync waits rise sharply while overall read/write wait events, queue depths, and device service times balloon. Checkpoints and log-file switches become more frequent, yet archives lag and log directories expand because the storage system cannot sustain the throughput required to off-load segments. Data-file and temp-file access also slow down, causing mixed wait profiles where buffer-I/O, durability flush, and general read/write stalls appear together. From the application side, short OLTP transactions begin to time out, batch windows overrun, and even read-only statements intermittently pause when they need to extend undo or temp segments that share the stressed devices. Diagnostic tools show CPU utilization moderate, but both log-specific waits and device-level I/O waits dominate session snapshots, making the true primary bottleneck difficult to distinguish.

Causal Chain: Heavy write activity first drives the transaction-log subsystem toward its throughput ceiling; because the same or adjacent storage stack is already near capacity, log-flushes queue up behind other data and temp I/Os, further extending commit latency. The lengthened commit path forces background processes (checkpoints, archiver, replication capture) to work harder and more frequently, injecting additional synchronous and asynchronous I/O into an already saturated storage layer. Conversely, the storage-level saturation feeds back into the log pipeline: slow archive writes delay log-file reuse, causing log buffer pressure and more frequent log switches. The two bottlenecks thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop that magnifies latency, starves worker threads, and can ultimately halt forward progress if log space cannot be reclaimed.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
